concept.name: CQRS & Event Sourcing

relationships.description: Events connect write side to read projections.

reviewRecord.reviewNotes: Seeded for SPEC-062 pillar coverage matrix.

spark.summary: CQRS separates write-side command validation from read-side query projections, while Event Sourcing persists every state transition as an immutable append-only log of domain events rather than overwriting current rows.
spark.keyTakeaway: Use CQRS without Event Sourcing whenever read and write shapes diverge; adopt Event Sourcing only when an immutable audit log, temporal replay, or multi-projection architecture justifies handling eventual consistency and schema evolution.

concept.whyItMatters: Traditional CRUD architectures force a single normalized schema to serve both transactional invariant checks and complex denormalized UI/reporting queries, creating lock contention and N+1 join bottlenecks. Combining CQRS with Event Sourcing—used in financial ledgers (TigerBeetle, Stripe-style double-entry), collaborative editors, and high-throughput order books—gives you append-only write throughput, deterministic state replay for debugging/auditing, and independently scalable read models (PostgreSQL, Elasticsearch, Redis).
whenToUse: Financial ledgers, healthcare records, or compliance-heavy domains requiring a cryptographically or structurally immutable audit trail of every state change.
Systems with extreme read/write asymmetry (e.g., 100:1 reads to writes) where read queries need specialized denormalized views in Elasticsearch or Redis.
Domains needing time-travel queries, retroactive bug-fix replays, or spawning new downstream analytics projections from historical events.
whenNotToUse: Standard CRUD domains (user profiles, CMS, simple inventory) where overwriting the current row in PostgreSQL is simpler and faster.
Flows requiring immediate strong read-your-own-writes consistency across complex cross-aggregate views without extra client versioning.
Small teams lacking operational maturity for idempotent consumers, event schema upcasting, and projection lag monitoring.
keyPoints: CQRS (Command Query Responsibility Segregation) and Event Sourcing are orthogonal: you can run CQRS over a plain relational DB, and you can use Event Sourcing with synchronous projections.

On the write side, an Aggregate reconstructs its state by replaying its event stream (up to a snapshot), validates the Command's invariants, and appends new Events using optimistic concurrency (`expectedVersion`).
Read models (Projections) asynchronously tail the event store (via EventStoreDB subscriptions, Kafka, or Postgres CDC/Outbox) and update denormalized tables idempotently.
Snapshotting every N events (e.g., every 100–500 events) bounds aggregate hydration latency so long-lived streams do not degrade write p99.
Because events are immutable facts, schema changes cannot mutate old records; consumers use **upcasters** (versioned event transformers) or weak-schema deserializers.

examples.title: Double-Entry Payment Ledger with EventStoreDB & Projections
examples.scenario: A fintech settlement service processes 8,000 transfers/sec while compliance and merchant dashboards query 90-day balance summaries.
examples.outcome: Commands append `FundsReserved`, `TransferSettled`, and `FeeAssessed` events to an append-only stream with `expectedVersion` checks, while asynchronous workers project into PostgreSQL read tables and ClickHouse analytics without locking the write path.

examples.title: E-Commerce Order Fulfillment with Outbox + Elasticsearch
examples.scenario: Customer support needs instant full-text search across 50M orders by SKU, shipping status, and customer email, which caused heavy `LIKE` queries on the primary OLTP database.
examples.outcome: Separating the write model (PostgreSQL + Transactional Outbox) from an Elasticsearch read projection cut OLTP CPU by 62% and reduced search p95 from 1.4 s to 28 ms.

tradeOffs.pro: Decoupled async projections let write and read databases scale and fail independently.
tradeOffs.con: Introduces replication lag (typically 10–200 ms), meaning a user who submits a command may refresh and see stale data unless the UI tracks a `streamVersion` watermark.

tradeOffs.pro: Every historical state and the business reason ('why' it changed) is preserved forever for replay and debugging.
tradeOffs.con: Ad-hoc queries against raw event streams are painful; every new query shape requires writing and backfilling a dedicated projection.

tradeOffs.pro: Adding a new read-model column only requires replaying events into a new projection table.
tradeOffs.con: Renaming or splitting an existing event type requires maintaining backward-compatible upcasters for the lifetime of the store.

failureModes.name: Projection Lag & Stale Read-Your-Writes
failureModes.description: A burst of 50,000 events backs up the projection consumer, causing users to see outdated balances or missing orders right after a `200 OK` command.
failureModes.mitigation: Return the committed `streamPosition` in the command response and have read queries wait (briefly) or fall back to reading the aggregate until the projection reaches that checkpoint.

failureModes.name: Dual-Write Split-Brain
failureModes.description: Writing an event to PostgreSQL and publishing to Kafka in two separate calls fails midway, leaving the read model permanently out of sync.
failureModes.mitigation: Use a dedicated Event Store (EventStoreDB) as the single source of truth, or use the Transactional Outbox pattern with Debezium CDC.

failureModes.name: Non-Idempotent Projection Handlers
failureModes.description: At-least-once delivery replays an `OrderPaid` event after a worker crash, double-incrementing a merchant's total revenue counter.
failureModes.mitigation: Store the last processed `(streamId, eventNumber)` or `eventId` in the same transaction as the read-model update and skip duplicates.

failureModes.name: GDPR / Right-to-Erasure Conflict
failureModes.description: PII stored inside immutable events violates legal deletion requests.
failureModes.mitigation: Use **crypto-shredding**: encrypt PII fields with a per-user key stored in a mutable KMS/vault, and delete the key upon erasure request.

commonMistakes: Applying Event Sourcing across an entire monolith instead of isolating it to core subdomains that genuinely need auditability or temporal replay.
Designing 'CRUD events' (`UserUpdated`) instead of domain-meaningful events (`SubscriptionUpgraded`, `ShippingAddressCorrected`), losing business intent.
Calling external HTTP APIs or generating non-deterministic `time.Now()`/`uuid.New()` inside projection replay handlers.
Allowing aggregates to grow unboundedly across millions of events without snapshots or stream archiving (e.g., monthly account closing events).
Blocking synchronous HTTP responses while waiting for 5 downstream projections to finish updating.

sections.content:
## The idea

**CQRS** (Command Query Responsibility Segregation) splits an application's data model into two distinct paths: a **Command** side that validates business rules and mutates state, and a **Query** side that reads pre-shaped, denormalized views.

**Event Sourcing** changes *how* the Command side persists state. Instead of executing `UPDATE accounts SET balance = 150 WHERE id = 42`, it appends an immutable domain event (`MoneyDeposited{amount: 50}`) to an append-only log. Current state is simply the left-fold (`reduce`) of all events in that stream. When paired together, the write model focuses purely on invariant enforcement and optimistic concurrency, while asynchronous projectors continuously fold the event log into optimized read databases.

## Concrete walkthrough

Trace a `WithdrawFunds(accountId='acc-9', amount=40)` command:

1. **Hydrate**: The command handler loads `snapshot@v100 (balance=120)` plus events `v101..v103` (`-10`, `+20`, `-30`), folding them to `currentBalance = 100`, `version = 103`.
2. **Validate**: Since `100 >= 40`, the aggregate emits `[FundsWithdrawn{amount: 40, txId: 'tx-77'}]`. (No DB mutation happens inside the domain object.)
3. **Atomic Append**: The repository appends the event to stream `acc-9` with `expectedVersion = 103`. If another concurrent request already wrote `v104`, the store rejects with `WrongExpectedVersion` (HTTP 409).
4. **Project**: The `AccountSummaryProjector` tails the global event log (`$all`), sees `v104`, verifies `last_checkpoint < global_pos` inside a PostgreSQL transaction, executes `UPDATE account_views SET balance = balance - 40, last_pos = ...`, and commits.

edges.title: Aggregate hydration
edges.description: Reads latest snapshot and subsequent events to reconstruct current in-memory state.

edges.label: 2. Append(expectedVersion)

edges.description: Appends new domain events if stream version matches; rejects concurrent conflicts.

edges.label: 3. Stream / CDC
edges.title: Ordered log delivery
edges.description: Pushes committed events in global commit order via subscription or outbox CDC.

edges.label: 4. Idempotent upsert
edges.title: Update read view + checkpoint
edges.description: Applies projection logic and records global offset in the same transaction.

edges.label: 5. Query / UI read
edges.title: Fast zero-join reads
edges.description: Clients query pre-computed read tables without touching the write-side event log.

data.caption: CQRS + Event Sourcing decouples transactional appends from asynchronous, idempotent read-model projections.

sections.content:
## Consistency, versioning & snapshots

Event-sourced systems trade immediate global consistency for **stream-level linearizability** plus **eventual read consistency**.
- **Write-side concurrency**: Optimistic concurrency (`expectedVersion`) guarantees no two commands overwrite each other on the same aggregate. Cross-aggregate invariants (e.g., transferring funds between two accounts) are coordinated via Sagas/Process Managers rather than distributed 2PC.
- **Read-your-own-writes**: Commands return `ETag: "v104"` or `X-Min-Position: 98412`. The query API polls or waits briefly for the projection checkpoint `>= 98412` before serving the requesting client.
- **Snapshotting**: A separate background worker periodically serializes aggregate state at `v500`, `v1000`, etc., keeping write-side hydration bounded to O(100) events.

## Architecture pattern comparison

| Pattern | Write Storage | Read Storage | Consistency | Audit Trail | Operational Complexity |
| :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- |
| **Standard CRUD** | Normalized OLTP | Same OLTP | Strong (ACID) | Manual audit table | Low |
| **CQRS + State DB** | Normalized OLTP | Replica / Elastic via CDC | Eventual reads | Optional | Medium |
| **CQRS + Event Sourcing** | Append-only Event Log | Multiple Projections | Stream-strong, read-eventual | Native & immutable | High (upcasting, replay) |

## Failure modes

1. **Poison-pill event**: A malformed or un-upcasted event crashes the projector in an infinite retry loop, stalling all downstream read updates. *Fix*: Dead-letter queue (DLQ) per stream or alertable circuit breaker after N retries.
2. **Blue/green projection rebuilds**: Rebuilding a 500M-event projection in-place breaks live reads. *Fix*: Write to a versioned table (`orders_v2`), catch up to live tail, then atomically swap the DB view/alias.
3. **Eventual consistency surprises**: Automated tests or UIs immediately `GET` after `POST` and see 404. *Fix*: Propagate causal position tokens or return the updated state summary in the command response.
4. **Side effects during replay**: Sending emails or charging cards inside a projection handler re-executes during a historical rebuild. *Fix*: Isolate external side effects to a live-only Process Manager that checks `isLiveMode` or deduplicates via idempotency keys.

## Schema evolution & GDPR

Because historical events are immutable facts, you never run `UPDATE events SET payload = ...`. Instead:
- **Additive changes**: Add optional fields with defaults.
- **Breaking changes**: Introduce `OrderPlacedV2` and register an **Upcaster** (`V1 -> V2`) in the deserialization pipeline before events reach aggregates or projections.
- **GDPR Erasure**: Store PII (name, email, SSN) encrypted with a per-subject AES-256 key (`user_key_42`) held in a separate mutable key store. Deleting `user_key_42` renders all historical PII fields cryptographically unreadable without breaking event-stream hashes or structural replay.

## Practical checklist

- [ ] Confirm Event Sourcing is restricted to bounded contexts that require auditability, replay, or temporal queries.
- [ ] Enforce optimistic concurrency (`expectedVersion`) on every event append.
- [ ] Guarantee atomic write + publish via an Event Store or Transactional Outbox + CDC (never dual-write).
- [ ] Make every projection handler idempotent using `(streamId, eventNumber)` or global log position checkpoints.
- [ ] Implement crypto-shredding for any PII stored inside immutable event payloads.
- [ ] Test full projection rebuilds from event 0 into a shadow table before going to production.

simulation.title: Interactive Simulation: Cqrs And Event Sourcing

steps.title: 1. Normal Request Ingress
steps.explanation: CQRS separates write-side command validation from read-side query projections, while Event Sourcing persists every state transition as an immutable append-only log of domain events rather than overwriting current rows.

steps.title: 2. Core Execution & State Lookup
steps.explanation: Async Projector applies the primary invariant and coordinates with Denormalized Read Model.

steps.title: 3. Scale Spike / Failure Injection
steps.explanation: Under a 10x burst, Denormalized Read Model experiences contention and tail-latency amplification.

steps.title: 4. Mitigation & Steady Recovery
steps.explanation: Return the committed `streamPosition` in the command response and have read queries wait (briefly) or fall back to reading the aggregate until the projection reaches that checkpoint.

tipsAndTricks: Core mental model: Use CQRS without Event Sourcing whenever read and write shapes diverge; adopt Event Sourcing only when an immutable audit log, temporal replay, or multi-projection architecture justifies handling eventual consistency and schema evolution.
Avoid trap: Applying Event Sourcing across an entire monolith instead of isolating it to core subdomains that genuinely need auditability or temporal replay.
Avoid trap: Designing 'CRUD events' (`UserUpdated`) instead of domain-meaningful events (`SubscriptionUpgraded`, `ShippingAddressCorrected`), losing business intent.
When to reach for it: Financial ledgers, healthcare records, or compliance-heavy domains requiring a cryptographically or structurally immutable audit trail of every state change.
When to reach for it: Systems with extreme read/write asymmetry (e.g., 100:1 reads to writes) where read queries need specialized denormalized views in Elasticsearch or Redis.

putItTogether.title: Putting Cqrs And Event Sourcing Together
putItTogether.summary: Use CQRS without Event Sourcing whenever read and write shapes diverge; adopt Event Sourcing only when an immutable audit log, temporal replay, or multi-projection architecture justifies handling eventual consistency and schema evolution.
steps: Establish baseline invariants for Cqrs And Event Sourcing before scaling.
Isolate hot paths with caching, backpressure, or partitioning.
Verify failure modes with synthetic load & chaos checks.
putItTogether.outcome: Commands append `FundsReserved`, `TransferSettled`, and `FeeAssessed` events to an append-only stream with `expectedVersion` checks, while asynchronous workers project into PostgreSQL read tables and ClickHouse analytics without locking the write path.
